dated_fact: For the gap: BLS payroll data (pulled from FRED on Nov 27, 2026, data through Oct 2026) show the test was met in 18 months between Nov 2023 and Dec 2025 and never before in the series, so the event is possible outside a recession. Against the gap: the last hit was Dec 2025; in Oct 2026 office payrolls were 51,000 above a year earlier; and the BLS Employment Projections 2025 to 2035 (table dated Aug 27, 2026) project growth in information (+5.3%), finance and insurance (+2.3%) and professional, scientific and technical services (+8.6%). No official forecast or filed figure points to a 200,000 fall in 2028 to 2029.
source: BLS CES via FRED, series USINFO, USFIRE, USPBS, PAYEMS, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/USPBS ; BLS Employment Projections, employment by major industry sector, https://www.bls.gov/emp/tables/employment-by-major-industry-sector.htm
note: I rebuilt the stored base rate from FRED and got the same count: 36 of 1,025 rolling 18-month windows (4%); since 1990 it is 36 of 425 (8%); for windows that start 18 months after the origin date, as this one does, 36 of 407 since 1990 (9%). Same test, same window length, so it is comparable. Two cautions: (1) the test reads each report as released, but the base rate uses today's revised series, and benchmark revisions made 2024 look worse than the first prints did; (2) a fixed 200,000 threshold was a far bigger share of office jobs before 1990, so 8 to 9 is the fairer comparator than 4. Halfway from 62 is 33 against 4, or 35 to 36 against 8 to 9. The recent run justifies part of the gap, not all of it, so I use the default 33. The odds_text still says 56% while odds_now is 62.

note: FIX BASE RATE: 24 to 41. dated_fact: Yen leg: Japan's Ministry of Finance bought yen on six days in 2026 (Apr 30, May 4, May 6, Jul 30, Jul 31, Aug 3), and the dollar was at 158.76 yen on Nov 20, 2026 against 163.86 on Jul 29, the day before the last round. 10-year leg: the 10-year closed at 5.31% on Oct 5, 2026 and 4.85% on Nov 25, 2026, and the Fed raised its target range on Sep 17, 2026 (upper bound 3.75% to 4.00%). These lift each leg above its history, but they do not make the joint event as likely as its weaker leg.
source: Japan MOF intervention history, https://www.mof.go.jp/english/policy/international_policy/reference/feio/foreign_exchange_intervention_operations.csv ; FRED DGS10, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS10 ; FRED DFEDTARU, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU ; FRED DEXJPUS, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DEXJPUS
note: Rebuilt from FRED and the MOF file with a 368-day horizon (Nov 27, 2026 to Nov 30, 2027): joint event in 716 of 8,669 starts since Apr 1991 (8%), all from the 1990s when the 10-year already sat above 5.50%. From starts with the 10-year within 25 bp of today's 4.85%: 10-year leg 149 of 708 (21%), joint 0 of 708. A plain 65 bp climb within the horizon happened in 40% of all starts since 1991, so our 43 for the 10-year leg is inside the range of history. The fault is the rule 'the lower leg binds': a joint event equals its lower leg only if the other leg is certain whenever the first fires. Our own legs (43 and 65) give 28 if independent, more if a yield spike drags the yen down with it. Default halfway from 43.1 to 8 is 26, close to that 28, so I keep the default. The one_number_rule text on the node should be changed.
